definition.text: A description of a game as a table (payoff matrix) listing each player's possible strategies and the payoffs for every combination of them.

facts.text: Each cell gives the row player's payoff first and the column player's second.
It suits games where players move at the same time or cannot see each other's move first.
It makes dominated strategies and Nash equilibria easy to spot, but loses some information compared with the extensive form.
In the prisoner's dilemma matrix, Defect beats Cooperate whatever the other does, so (Defect, Defect) is the only Nash equilibrium.
A sequential game can be written in normal form only by listing every contingent plan, including for situations that never arise.
Every extensive-form game has an equivalent normal form, though converting can make the representation exponentially larger.

definition.text: A game made of the same base game (the stage game) played over and over by the same players.

facts.text: Repetition makes players weigh how today's action affects others' future actions, an effect sometimes called reputation.
Two neighbouring petrol stations would both earn zero profit in a one-off price war, yet they make profits because they meet again every day.
Repeating the same game a finite or an infinite number of times can lead to very different equilibria and best strategies.
In the infinitely repeated prisoner's dilemma the preferred strategy is to cooperate rather than play the one-shot Nash strategy.
Sustaining cooperation relies on punishing anyone who deviates; results showing which outcomes can be sustained are the folk theorems.
A game repeated an unknown number of times is treated like an infinitely repeated one, since there is no known last round.

definition.text: A repeated-game strategy that cooperates until the other player deviates and then punishes them with play that lowers both players' payoffs.

facts.text: Knowing the other follows a trigger strategy, a player expects lower future payoffs if they act selfishly now.
An effective trigger makes cooperating worth more than grabbing a gain now and suffering punishment later.
The harshest form, grim trigger, punishes forever and is used to prove the folk theorem.

definition.text: A repeated game played for a fixed, known number of rounds, with each player's total payoff the sum over all rounds.

facts.text: If the stage game has a single Nash equilibrium, players play it in every round: reasoning backward from the last round unravels any cooperation.
A known, finite end therefore undermines cooperation in every round; cooperation is possible only when the number of rounds is infinite or unknown.
If the stage game has several equilibria, the threat of switching to a worse one later can support cooperation in earlier rounds.

definition.text: A method of fairly dividing the total gains or costs of a group effort among its members according to each one's average contribution.

facts.text: It looks at how much the result changes when a player joins every possible combination of others, then averages those changes.
Lloyd Shapley introduced it in 1951.
It is the only division satisfying efficiency, symmetry, additivity and the null-player property, widely accepted as defining fairness.
Efficiency means all the group's gain is shared out; a player who adds nothing to any coalition gets zero.
If cooperation creates positive synergy, every member gains at least what they could get alone.
It is used to divide business profits and to measure each feature's importance in machine-learning models and sensitivity analysis.

definition.text: An extension of the Shapley value to games with a continuum of players, each of whom plays only a tiny role.

facts.text: Lloyd Shapley and Robert Aumann created it in their 1974 book; Jean-François Mertens and Abraham Neyman extended it further.
